title: Bhishma Waits for the Sun
hookLine: Bhishma, on a bed of arrows, waits for the sun to turn north: Hindus hold the turn sacred, and Ayurveda reads the same two halves in the body
carry: the sun's turn north is held sacred
tomorrow: why did the god of fire lose his appetite?

cards: The greatest warrior of the Mahabharata has fallen. Bhishma, the old grandfather of both armies, lies on the battlefield held up by arrows, so many that his body doesn't touch the ground. He could die now.
Long ago he was given a boon: he can choose his own time. And he chooses to wait. For the sun.

teach.b: Bhishma waits, the epic says, for many nights, until the sun turns north. While he waits, the Pandavas come to his bed of arrows, and he teaches them: the long talks of the Shanti book, on kingship, dharma and freedom.
Then the sun turns, and he lets go. Uttarayana, the sun's northern course, is held as sacred time; the Gita names its six months among the signs of the path that leads to Brahman.
Hindus celebrate the turn with Makar Sankranti in January: kites, sesame sweets, holy dips in rivers. Here's the teaching.
Hindus see time itself as sacred, and the sun's two journeys, north and south, shape the religious year. Ayurveda reads the same sky in the body.
The Charaka Samhita calls the northern half adana, the taking: the sun and the wind grow sharp and dry and draw strength out of the world and out of people.
The southern half is visarga, the giving: the moon is strong, the earth is cooled by clouds and rain, and strength flows back.
People are weakest, it says, where the taking ends and the giving begins, around the end of summer and the first rains. Today, that's a kinder way to read a low stretch.

teach.h: A LOW SEASON ISN'T A FAILING
teach.b: A drained late summer isn't a flaw in your character; on this lens, the year itself has a taking half. And Bhishma shows what a wait can hold: even on a bed of arrows, he used it to teach.

how: Hindus celebrate the sun's turn at Makar Sankranti with kites, sesame sweets and river dips, and many hold uttarayana, the sun's northern course, as an auspicious time; Ayurvedic practitioners call the two halves of the year adana and visarga and adjust diet and activity to them.

o: the months when fasting is asked of everyone
a year in two halves: one takes strength, one gives it
a calendar of the dates when festivals must fall

games.q: the sun's two courses — tap the pairs.
p: waited for the sun's turn north

s: Bhishma chose to wait for uttarayana before he died
he had the boon to choose his time, and taught the Pandavas while he waited.
Makar Sankranti has nothing to do with the sun
it celebrates the sun's turn, with kites, sesame sweets and river dips.
Charaka says people are strongest at the end of summer
weakest where the taking half ends, around the end of summer and the first rains.

games.q: it's the end of a long, hot summer and you feel drained. how does the Charaka Samhita read it?
o: the taking half of the year, at its low point.
games.why: the text places weakness where adana, the taking, turns into visarga, the giving: around the end of summer and the start of the rains.

practice: Many Hindus greet the morning sun with folded hands, some offering a little water toward it. Turn toward the light wherever you are, even a window, and fold your hands.

Breathe out slowly, letting go of what this season has taken; breathe in, letting strength come back, with no forcing. If you pray, you can say Om Suryaya namah, a greeting to the sun; if you don't, simply feel the light.

wordCard.voice: The seasons. The sun's two courses: adana, the taking, while it goes north, and visarga, the giving, while it goes south.

orig.note: Sanskrit adana: taking. In Ayurveda, the half of the year while the sun travels its northern course.

carryVoice: Your line: the sun's turn north is held sacred. Bhishma waited for it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva (Bhishma falls onto a bed of arrows and resolves to wait for the sun's northern course); Shanti and Anushasana Parvas (his teaching to the Pandavas; his death when the sun turns north)
Bhagavad Gita 8.24 (fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course: those who depart then go to Brahman)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 6.4–8 (the year in two halves, adana and visarga, with the sun's northern and southern courses; the qualities of sun, wind and moon in each; strength through the year)
Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 3.2–7 (uttarayana as adana, dakshinayana as visarga)
